front: Why can't mlx-lm 0.32 run on the Python that came with the Mac?
back: It needs Python 3.11 or newer. The Mac came with 3.9.

front: In the name Qwen3.5-4B-4bit, what do 4B and 4bit mean?
back: About 4 billion parameters. Each weight stored in about 4 bits.

front: What does 4-bit quantization trade?
back: A little accuracy, for a model about a third of the size and memory.

front: A reasoning model returned no answer within the token limit. What happened?
back: Its thinking used the whole token budget. Raise the limit or turn thinking off.

front: Why download models only from accounts you can identify?
back: Impostor accounts publish altered copies under real model names.

front: What does LoRA train?
back: Small added low-rank matrices. The original weights stay frozen.

front: What is in a LoRA adapter file?
back: Only the trained added weights. Megabytes, loaded on top of the unchanged base model.

front: Training loss fell. Does that prove the model got better at the task?
back: No. Only a held-out test set, scored before and after, can show that.

front: What is a majority-class baseline?
back: The score from always answering the most common label. Here: always "Health", 8.0% on the golden set.

front: How do House and Senate companions stay out of different splits?
back: Companions often differ only in 'A bill to'. The key strips it, and short titles join reworded ones, so companions share a split.

front: Why is the golden set committed to git instead of rebuilt each time?
back: The public record changes daily. A frozen set makes every score comparable to every other.

front: What does a stratified test set guarantee?
back: Every label with enough examples appears, here at least twice, so rare labels are tested too.

front: How does the harness treat a reply it cannot parse into a label?
back: As invalid: counted wrong and reported separately. Never dropped, or dodging hard cases would raise accuracy.

front: What does macro-F1 add over accuracy?
back: It averages F1 across labels equally, so failing on a small label hurts as much as a big one.

front: Why is Qwen3.5's thinking turned off for this eval?
back: Thinking cost 1,500+ tokens and about 20 seconds per bill, and could run out of room before answering.

front: How is cost per 1,000 bills computed?
back: Measured input and output tokens times per-token prices given at run time, scaled to 1,000 bills.

front: Which error group can a fine-tune fix, and which can it not?
back: It can learn labelling conventions, like tax-code bills being Taxation. It cannot recover facts a thin title never states.

front: What does the CI gate check, given that it runs no model?
back: It re-scores committed predictions against frozen golden labels, checks the golden file's checksum, and fails below the bar.

front: Why does the gate take gold labels from the golden file, not the predictions file?
back: So a predictions file cannot grade itself by rewriting its own gold labels.

front: What stops a paid eval run from overspending?
back: --max-usd refuses a run whose worst case is too high. It protects you when you pass the real prices.

front: What is the difference between full fine-tuning and LoRA?
back: Full fine-tuning changes every weight. LoRA freezes them and trains small added matrices.

front: One base model, ten tasks. What does LoRA let you store?
back: One base model and ten small adapters, swapped at load time.

front: Why cap the number of training examples per label?
back: Uncapped, the model sees common labels far more often and guesses them when unsure.

front: Why can a fine-tuned classifier use a prompt with no label list?
back: It learned the label names from the training replies, so they need not be repeated.

front: What must never appear in the training data?
back: Any example from the test set, including the same bill under a different title.

front: What mainly drives memory use while training on a Mac?
back: The number of tokens in one batch: batch size times example length.

front: What does gradient accumulation do?
back: It adds up gradients over several small batches before one update. Bigger effective batch, same memory.

front: Training loss bounces while validation loss falls. Which do you trust?
back: Validation loss. It is measured on the same held-out examples every time.

front: Two models were scored with different prompts. When is that comparison fair?
back: When both use the same test set and parser, and the table names each prompt.

front: On a 150-example test set, how much is one example worth?
back: About 0.7 points. A gap of two or three examples is noise.

front: A converted model's license tag disagrees with the original's. Which counts?
back: The original's. Read the license where the lab that made the model published it.

front: Why does a good model card list the model's limits?
back: A reader will find them anyway. Naming them shows the model was tested, not only trained.
